In [[queueing theory]], the '''Engset formula''' is used to determine the blocking probability of an M/M/c/c/N queue (in [[Kendall's notation]]).

The formula is named after its developer, [[T. O. Engset]].

==Example application==

Consider a fleet of <math>c</math> vehicles and <math>N</math> operators. Operators enter the system randomly to request the use of a vehicle.
If no vehicles are available, a requesting operator is "blocked" (i.e., the operator leaves without a vehicle).
The owner of the fleet would like to pick <math>c</math> small so as to minimize costs, but large enough to ensure that the blocking probability is tolerable.

==Formula==

Let

* <math>c > 0</math> be the (integer) number of servers.
* <math>N > c</math> be the (integer) number of sources of traffic;
* <math>\lambda > 0</math> be the idle source arrival rate (i.e., the rate at which a free source initiates requests);
* <math>h > 0</math> be the average holding time (i.e., the average time it takes for a server to handle a request);

Then, the [[probability]] of blocking is given by<ref name="Tijms2003">{{cite book|last1=Tijms|first1=Henk C.|year=2003|title=A first course in stochastic models|publisher=John Wiley and Sons|doi=10.1002/047001363X}}</ref>
:<math>P=\frac{\binom{N-1}{c}\left(\lambda h\right)^{c}}{\sum_{i=0}^{c}\binom{N-1}{i}\left(\lambda h\right)^{i}}.</math>
By rearranging terms, one can rewrite the above formula as<ref name="AzimzadehCarpenter2016">{{cite journal|last1=Azimzadeh|first1=Parsiad|last2=Carpenter|first2=Tommy|title=Fast Engset computation|journal=Operations Research Letters|volume=44|issue=3|year=2016|pages=313–318|issn=0167-6377|doi=10.1016/j.orl.2016.02.011|arxiv = 1511.00291}}</ref>
:<math>P = \frac{1}{ {}_2 F_1(1,-c;N-c;-1/(\lambda h) ) }</math>
where <math>{}_2 F_1</math> is the Gaussian [[hypergeometric function]].

===Computation===

There are several recursions<ref name="Zukerman">{{cite web|last=Zukerman|first=Moshe|title=An Introduction to Queueing Theory and Stochastic Teletraffic Models|date=2000|url=http://www.ee.cityu.edu.hk/~zukerman/classnotes.pdf|format=pdf|accessdate=2012-11-27}}</ref> that can be used to compute <math>P</math> in a numerically stable manner.

Alternatively, any numerical package that supports the [[hypergeometric function]] can be used. Some examples are given below.

'''[[Python (programming language)|Python]] with [[SciPy]]'''
<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
from scipy.special import hyp2f1
P = 1.0 / hyp2f1(1, -c, N - c, -1.0 / (Lambda * h))
</syntaxhighlight>

'''[[MATLAB]] with the [http://www.mathworks.com/products/symbolic/ Symbolic Math Toolbox]'''
<syntaxhighlight lang="matlab">
P = 1 / hypergeom([1, -c], N - c, -1 / (Lambda * h))
</syntaxhighlight>

==Unknown source arrival rate==

In practice, it is often the case that the source arrival rate <math>\lambda</math> is unknown (or hard to estimate) while <math>\alpha > 0</math>, the [[Erlang (unit)|offered traffic]] per-source, is known.
In this case, one can substitute the relationship
:<math>\lambda h=\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha(1-P)}</math>
between the source arrival rate and blocking probability into the Engset formula to arrive at the fixed point equation
:<math>P = f(P)</math>
where
:<math>f(P) = \frac{1}{ {}_2 F_1(1,-c;N-c;1-P-1/\alpha) }.</math>

===Computation===

While the above removes the unknown <math>\lambda</math> from the formula, it introduces an additional point of complexity: we can no longer compute the blocking probability directly, and must use an [[iterative method]] instead. While a [[fixed-point iteration]] is tempting, it has been shown that such an iteration is sometimes [[Limit of a sequence|divergent]] when applied to <math>f</math>.<ref name="AzimzadehCarpenter2016" /> Alternatively, it is possible to use one of [[bisection]] or [[Newton's method]], for which an [https://github.com/parsiad/fast-engset/releases open source implementation] is available.
